entries.title: Anarchism
entries.text: Anarchism is the idea that people can organize their lives without rulers: without a state, bosses or any authority that can't justify itself to the people it affects. Pierre-Joseph Proudhon was the first to call himself an anarchist, in What Is Property? (1840). Anarchists don't mean disorder. They mean order from below, made by free association, mutual aid and federation instead of command. Most anarchists of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries were also socialists: they wanted the land and the workshops held in common, and saw the state and capital as two halves of one system of domination.
entries.game: You play the movement, not a government. The communes run themselves; you can only persuade, propose and back. The game's central danger, hierarchy drift, is the anarchist fear that a revolution can rebuild the power it overthrew.
reading: Colin Ward, Anarchy in Action (1973)
Peter Marshall, Demanding the Impossible (1992)
Errico Malatesta, Anarchy (1891)

entries.title: The many anarchisms
entries.text: Anarchists have never agreed on everything. Anarcho-syndicalists (the CNT in Spain) put their hope in revolutionary unions; anarchist communists (Kropotkin, Malatesta) in communes sharing according to need; individualists (Max Stirner, Benjamin Tucker) in the sovereign individual and voluntary exchange; Christian and pacifist anarchists (Tolstoy) in refusing all violence. In the 1920s, exiles from the Russian Revolution split over the Organizational Platform (1926), which called for a disciplined anarchist organization with a common program, against the 'synthesis' of Voline and Sébastien Faure, which wanted a loose union of all tendencies. Anarcha-feminists, from Emma Goldman to the Spanish Mujeres Libres, insisted that domination at home and in the family was as real as domination by the state.
entries.game: This game models one tradition: the anarcho-syndicalist and anarchist-communist movements of Spain, Ukraine and France, organized in federated communes. Other anarchisms would make a different game.
reading: Peter Marshall, Demanding the Impossible (1992)
Robert Graham (ed.), Anarchism: A Documentary History of Libertarian Ideas (2005–2012)

entries.title: Mutual aid
entries.text: Peter Kropotkin's Mutual Aid: A Factor of Evolution (1902) answered the Social Darwinists who read nature as a war of all against all. In animals and in human history, from village communes to medieval guilds and workers' societies, he found cooperation as important to survival as competition. Anarchists took from it the conviction that people can sustain a society by sharing and helping one another, without being made to.
entries.game: Communes share food and goods with neighbours they trust, and send militia to help them at the front. Trust is the federation's real strength: it carries help, ideas and support, and it is what keeps communes from leaving.
reading: Peter Kropotkin, Mutual Aid: A Factor of Evolution (1902)

entries.title: Federation and free association
entries.text: Anarchists proposed to replace the state with federations: communes and unions joined from below, each free to govern itself, linked by agreements they can leave. Proudhon set the idea out in The Principle of Federation (1863), and Bakunin built his programs on it. Coordination flows up through delegates who carry their community's decisions and can be recalled, never down by command. Its critics asked whether a federation could act fast enough in war or plan an economy; its defenders answered that centralization was the danger, not the cure.
entries.game: The federation is the communes that choose to belong. A discontented commune can vote to leave; holding it by force is possible, but it breaks trust and adds drift. Projects are joined by invitation, and coordinating many communes costs effort.
reading: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, The Principle of Federation (1863)
Mikhail Bakunin, Statism and Anarchy (1873)

entries.title: Against the state
entries.text: For anarchists the state is not a neutral tool that can be captured and used for good: it is a minority holding the means of force over a majority, and whoever takes it over becomes that minority. This was the heart of the split with Marx in the First International (1872). In Statism and Anarchy (1873) Bakunin predicted that a 'people's state' would be ruled by a new class of educated administrators, governing in the people's name. Many anarchists read the Russian Revolution as proof.
entries.game: If drift reaches its last stage, a state crystallizes out of the councils and commissars: the game ends with the revolution lost, even if the war was won.
reading: Mikhail Bakunin, Statism and Anarchy (1873)
Emma Goldman, My Disillusionment in Russia (1923)

entries.title: Means and ends
entries.text: Anarchists insist that the way a revolution is made shapes what it becomes: you cannot reach freedom through dictatorship, or equality through a disciplined hierarchy. Malatesta argued it for fifty years; Emma Goldman concluded from Russia that 'no revolution can ever succeed as a factor of liberation unless the means used to further it be identical in spirit and tendency with the purposes to be achieved'. Today this is often called prefigurative politics: organizing now in the form of the society you want.
entries.game: Almost every shortcut in the game — the war committee, government arms, foreign advisers, conscription, the statistics bureau — works, and costs drift. The game asks the anarchists' question: how much can you borrow from the methods of the state before you become one?
reading: Emma Goldman, My Disillusionment in Russia (1923), Afterword
Errico Malatesta, writings collected in The Method of Freedom (2014)

entries.title: Anarcho-syndicalism
entries.text: Anarcho-syndicalists made the union the seed of the new society: workers organized by trade and industry would fight the bosses through direct action and the general strike, and one day take over production themselves. The French CGT's Charter of Amiens (1906) and Spain's CNT (founded 1910) were its great organizations; by 1936 the CNT had well over a million members. Rudolf Rocker's Anarcho-Syndicalism (1938) is its classic statement.
entries.game: The Catalan scenario's industrial communes are syndicates (Sants textile workers, Poblenou metalworkers), and the general strike can come as an event that stalls the enemy's supply.
reading: Rudolf Rocker, Anarcho-Syndicalism: Theory and Practice (1938)

entries.title: Libertarian communism
entries.text: Kropotkin's The Conquest of Bread (1892) argued that once the land and the workshops were taken back, a free society could provide for everyone from common stores: 'from each according to ability, to each according to need', without money or wages. In May 1936 the CNT's Zaragoza congress adopted a program of libertarian communism built on free communes; within weeks, parts of Aragon and Catalonia were trying to live it.
entries.game: Communes produce food and goods and share them through trust; prices only rise as scarcity bites, and trade abroad for currency brings accounts and markets back in, which counts as drift.
reading: Peter Kropotkin, The Conquest of Bread (1892)
Isaac Puente, Libertarian Communism (1932)

entries.title: The assembly
entries.text: In anarchist practice decisions are made by those they affect, in open assemblies of a village, a workplace or a neighbourhood, not by representatives ruling in their name. The assembly decides; anyone it chooses to carry its decisions elsewhere is a delegate, not a leader. Assemblies are slow and demanding, and anarchists have argued ever since about how to make them work at scale.
entries.game: The technology 'Open assemblies' makes decisions bind only those who make them, and slows federal decisions. Many communes' own proposals reach you as their assembly's request.
reading: Murray Bookchin, The Next Revolution (2015)
Colin Ward, Anarchy in Action (1973)

entries.title: The imperative mandate and recall
entries.text: A delegate in an anarchist federation carries a mandate: instructions from the assembly that sent them, which they may not exceed. If they betray it they can be recalled at once. The Paris Commune of 1871 made its members 'revocable at any moment', which Marx too praised; the CNT's congresses voted by delegates mandated by their unions. The point is that power stays with the base, and nobody becomes indispensable.
entries.game: Recall delegates breaks up informal power: drift falls, but experience is lost and defence suffers briefly. Mandates, recall and rotation brake drift every turn.
reading: Karl Marx, The Civil War in France (1871)
José Peirats, The CNT in the Spanish Revolution (1951–53)

entries.title: Rotation
entries.text: Rotating tasks and posts keeps any one person from accumulating the knowledge, contacts and habits of command that turn a delegate into a boss. It costs: newcomers know less, and things are done less well for a while. Anarchists have generally thought the price worth paying.
entries.game: Figures who have gathered a following can be rotated back to the ranks: their followers grumble, and the power they were gathering is broken up. Delegates are recalled and replaced by rotation when drift nears a threshold.
reading: Robert Michels, Political Parties (1911) — the problem rotation answers

entries.title: Ateneos and rationalist schools
entries.text: Spanish anarchists built a culture of their own: ateneos libertarios (workers' athenaeums with libraries, literacy classes and debates), newspapers, theatre, hiking clubs. Francisco Ferrer's Escuela Moderna (1901) taught children without church or state; Ferrer was executed in 1909, and his schools inspired others across Europe and the Americas. The idea was that people who can read, argue and decide together don't need rulers, and won't put up with them.
entries.game: Political education is your main brake on drift. Political schools, pamphlets, ateneo networks and cultural works raise it; practical schooling raises production, but if it runs ahead of political education experts start to take charge.
reading: Francisco Ferrer, The Origin and Ideals of the Modern School (1913)
Paul Avrich, The Modern School Movement (1980)

entries.title: Collectivization
entries.text: After July 1936, workers in Catalonia took over factories, trams, railways and public services, and peasants in Aragon, the Levante and Andalusia formed collectives: perhaps several hundred in Aragon alone. Some abolished money and shared by need; others kept a family wage. They varied greatly, and historians still debate how voluntary and how productive they were. In August 1937 the Republic's own troops broke up many of the Aragon collectives.
entries.game: Collectivizing the works is a project the communes propose once the war allows it: one plan for every collective, with the efficiency and the risk that a plan brings planners.
reading: Gaston Leval, Collectives in the Spanish Revolution (1975)
Sam Dolgoff (ed.), The Anarchist Collectives (1974)

entries.title: Militias
entries.text: In July 1936 the CNT's workers defeated the military rising in Barcelona and formed columns of volunteers, such as Durruti's, which elected their delegates, held assemblies and had no saluting or ranks. Their supporters saw a new kind of army; their critics, an undisciplined one. From late 1936 the Republic 'militarized' the militias into a regular army with officers, and the anarchists argued bitterly over whether to accept it. In Ukraine, Makhno's insurgent army kept elected commanders throughout.
entries.game: Each commune's militia is its people under arms, their militancy and spirit; neighbours send help by trust. Elected officers and militia doctrine are techniques; government arms come with militarization.
reading: George Orwell, Homage to Catalonia (1938)
Abel Paz, Durruti in the Spanish Revolution (1996)

entries.title: Hierarchy drift
entries.text: Why do organizations founded to free people so often end up ruled by a few? Bakunin warned of a 'red bureaucracy'. The sociologist Robert Michels, studying Germany's socialist party, called it the 'iron law of oligarchy' (1911): whoever organizes needs leaders, experts and officials, and these acquire knowledge, control of resources and interests of their own. Anarchists have answered with recall, rotation, education and the refusal of permanent office, while admitting that the pull never goes away.
entries.game: Drift is the game's measure of that pull. War, big projects, experts, popular figures, trade and emergency powers push it up; political education, recall, rotation and some techniques push it down. At 25 permanent councils form, at 50 commissars, at 75 a party; at the end, a state.
reading: Robert Michels, Political Parties (1911)
Mikhail Bakunin, Statism and Anarchy (1873)

entries.title: The expert trap
entries.text: Bakunin did not reject expertise: 'In the matter of boots, I refer to the authority of the bootmaker.' What he rejected was letting expertise become command: the engineer, the planner or the scientist deciding for everyone else. Anarchists thought the answer was to spread knowledge widely and keep experts answerable to those they serve.
entries.game: When a commune's practical education runs far ahead of its political education, experts start to take charge, and drift rises. The Needs attention list warns you; a political school helps.
reading: Mikhail Bakunin, God and the State (1882)

entries.title: Double-edged technology
entries.text: Some tools spread power; others concentrate it. The historian Lewis Mumford distinguished 'authoritarian' from 'democratic' technics (1964): a power grid or a telegraph network needs a centre and someone to run it, a workshop tool does not. Anarchists have long asked which technologies a free society can live with, and on what terms.
entries.game: Most technologies in the game carry a risk: the telegraph favours hub towns, newspapers make editors powerful, a grid needs a board. Each is useful and adds a little drift; free paths exist for some.
reading: Lewis Mumford, 'Authoritarian and Democratic Technics' (1964)
Murray Bookchin, Post-Scarcity Anarchism (1971)

entries.title: War or revolution?
entries.text: The Spanish anarchists faced a dilemma they never solved. To defeat Franco they needed arms, which the Republic and the Soviet Union would give only to a disciplined army under a central command. Accepting meant ministers, militarization and the slow end of the revolution; refusing meant losing the war. In September and November 1936 the CNT joined the Catalan and Spanish governments. Critics inside the movement, such as the Friends of Durruti, called it the abandonment of the revolution; its leaders called it the price of survival. Franco won anyway.
entries.game: Every arms offer, war committee and emergency measure is this dilemma in small. You can lose by being crushed, or by becoming a state.
reading: Vernon Richards, Lessons of the Spanish Revolution (1953)
Burnett Bolloten, The Spanish Civil War (1991)

entries.title: Parties and commissars
entries.text: Anarchists and Bolsheviks fought side by side against the old order in Russia and Spain, and then against each other. The Bolsheviks believed a disciplined party had to lead the revolution; anarchists that a party in power becomes a new ruling class. In 1921 the Red Army crushed the Kronstadt sailors who demanded free soviets, and the Cheka had already turned on Russia's anarchists. In Spain the Soviet advisers and the Communist party gained influence with every shipment of arms.
entries.game: Rival parties grow cells where political education is thin and life is hard. They offer arms for commissars, harder each time. Exposing their cells costs their patrons' goodwill.
reading: Voline, The Unknown Revolution (1947)
Paul Avrich, Kronstadt 1921 (1970)

entries.title: Leaders in a leaderless movement
entries.text: Anarchist movements rejected leaders, and produced famous ones anyway: Durruti, Makhno, Louise Michel, Federica Montseny. Their courage and skill mattered; so did the danger that a following becomes a power base. Anarchists tried to keep even their heroes answerable, with mixed success.
entries.game: Historical figures bring defence, influence or organization. Over time some gather a following and an appetite for office: you can let them take the power they ask for, or rotate them back to the ranks.
reading: Abel Paz, Durruti in the Spanish Revolution (1996)

entries.title: The Paris Commune, 1871
entries.text: After France's defeat by Prussia, Paris rose on 18 March 1871 when the government tried to take the National Guard's cannon. The city elected a Commune on 26 March: workers, artisans, journalists, Proudhonists, Blanquists and members of the International. In two months it separated church and state, ended night work in bakeries, handed abandoned workshops to cooperatives and made its members recallable. It never marched on Versailles while it could, and left the Bank of France untouched. On 1 May a majority voted a Committee of Public Safety over the minority's protest. From 21 to 28 May, Bloody Week, the Versailles army retook the city; many thousands were killed.
entries.game: The Paris scenario is the hardest: a short siege that ends in Bloody Week. Its decisions are the Commune's own debates.
reading: Prosper-Olivier Lissagaray, History of the Paris Commune of 1871 (1876)
Louise Michel, The Red Virgin: Memoirs (1886)

entries.title: The Free Territory, 1918–1921
entries.text: In southern Ukraine, around Huliaipole, peasants and workers led by Nestor Makhno fought the Austro-German occupiers, the nationalists, the White armies and finally the Bolsheviks. Regional congresses of peasants, workers and insurgents governed the area; land was taken by those who worked it, and the insurgent army elected its commanders. In June 1919 Trotsky's Order No. 1824 banned the insurgents' congress. In September 1919 the insurgents broke Denikin's White army at Peregonovka; in October 1920 they allied with the Red Army against Wrangel, and in November, Wrangel beaten, the Red Army turned on them. Makhno escaped abroad in 1921 and died in Paris in 1934.
entries.game: The Free Territory scenario: harsher than Catalonia, its decisions drawn from the insurgents' congresses and the Bolshevik alliance and betrayal.
reading: Peter Arshinov, History of the Makhnovist Movement (1923)
Alexandre Skirda, Nestor Makhno: Anarchy's Cossack (1982)

entries.title: Revolutionary Catalonia, 1936–1939
entries.text: When generals rose against the Spanish Republic on 17–19 July 1936, the CNT and other workers' organizations defeated them in Barcelona. For months power lay with the unions and a Central Committee of Antifascist Militias; factories and land were collectivized, and columns marched on Aragon. George Orwell found a city where 'the working class was in the saddle'. The CNT joined the Catalan and then the Spanish government; Durruti was killed at Madrid in November. In May 1937 street fighting in Barcelona (the May Days) broke the revolutionaries' power, and in August the Council of Aragon was dissolved by force. Barcelona fell to Franco in January 1939.
entries.game: The default scenario. You can be crushed by the Nationalists, or survive the war and become the state you fought.
reading: George Orwell, Homage to Catalonia (1938)
Abel Paz, Durruti in the Spanish Revolution (1996)
Chris Ealham, Anarchism and the City (2010)

entries.title: Elsewhere
entries.text: Anarchist and anarchist-influenced experiments reached far beyond the game's three scenarios: the Kronstadt sailors' free soviets (1921); the Korean anarchists' Shinmin autonomous region in Manchuria (1929–1931); the Spanish collectives of Aragon and the Levante; the Zapatista autonomous communities of Chiapas since 1994; and the democratic confederalism of north-east Syria, inspired by Murray Bookchin's municipalism. Several have entries of their own here. None is a pure model, and their histories are argued over; together they show the ideas being tried.
entries.game: The open world lets you raise the movement anywhere and in any age: alternate history, asking what these ideas might have done elsewhere.
reading: Murray Bookchin, The Next Revolution (2015)
Alex Khasnabish, Zapatismo Beyond Borders (2008)

entries.title: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon (1809–1865)
entries.text: A printer from Besançon, the first to call himself an anarchist. 'Property is theft!' he wrote in What Is Property? (1840), meaning property that lets its owner live from others' work. He proposed mutual credit, workers' associations and a federation of free communes in place of the state. His ideas shaped the French workers' movement and many Communards; his hostility to women's equality has been rightly condemned.
reading: Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, What Is Property? (1840)

entries.title: Mikhail Bakunin (1814–1876)
entries.text: A Russian revolutionary who fought on the barricades of 1848, spent years in Tsarist prisons and Siberian exile, and escaped to lead the anti-authoritarian wing of the First International against Marx. He predicted that a revolutionary state would breed a new ruling class, and gave anarchism its collectivist and federalist program.
reading: Mikhail Bakunin, Statism and Anarchy (1873)
Mikhail Bakunin, God and the State (1882)

entries.title: Peter Kropotkin (1842–1921)
entries.text: A Russian prince turned geographer and revolutionary, imprisoned in Russia and France, who spent most of his life in exile in England. He gave anarchist communism its theory in The Conquest of Bread (1892) and Mutual Aid (1902). He returned to Russia in 1917 and died there in 1921, critical of the Bolshevik dictatorship; tens of thousands followed his funeral, among the last anarchist demonstrations the Soviet authorities allowed.
reading: Peter Kropotkin, The Conquest of Bread (1892)
Peter Kropotkin, Mutual Aid (1902)

entries.title: Errico Malatesta (1853–1932)
entries.text: An Italian electrician and revolutionary, active for sixty years in Italy, Argentina, London and beyond. Less a system-builder than a practical thinker, he argued that anarchy is a method as much as a goal: freedom has to be practised now, and organization is necessary as long as it is voluntary. He died under house arrest in Fascist Rome.
reading: Errico Malatesta, Anarchy (1891)
Vernon Richards (ed.), Errico Malatesta: His Life and Ideas (1965)

entries.title: Emma Goldman (1869–1940)
entries.text: A Lithuanian-born anarchist in the United States, famous for her speeches and her journal Mother Earth, who campaigned for free speech, birth control and women's freedom and against conscription. Deported to Russia in 1919, she left it disillusioned in 1921 and wrote one of the first anarchist critiques of the Soviet state. She worked for the CNT during the Spanish Civil War, and died in Toronto in 1940.
reading: Emma Goldman, Living My Life (1931)
Emma Goldman, My Disillusionment in Russia (1923)

entries.title: Louise Michel (1830–1905)
entries.text: A schoolteacher who fought with the National Guard in the Paris Commune and ran an ambulance during Bloody Week. Deported to New Caledonia, she befriended the Kanak people and supported their revolt of 1878. She returned to France an anarchist and spent the rest of her life speaking for the cause, often from prison.
reading: Louise Michel, The Red Virgin: Memoirs of Louise Michel (1886)

entries.title: Nestor Makhno (1888–1934)
entries.text: A peasant from Huliaipole, imprisoned by the Tsar for his anarchist activity, who led the Revolutionary Insurrectionary Army of Ukraine through the civil war. A brilliant guerrilla commander, he fought every side that tried to rule the region, and was finally driven out by the Red Army in 1921. He died poor in Paris, where he had helped write the Organizational Platform.
reading: Nestor Makhno, The Russian Revolution in Ukraine (memoirs, 1929–1937)
Alexandre Skirda, Nestor Makhno: Anarchy's Cossack (1982)

entries.title: Buenaventura Durruti (1896–1936)
entries.text: A mechanic from León who became the CNT's best-known militant: a bank robber for the cause, an exile, a union organizer. In July 1936 he helped defeat the rising in Barcelona and led a column to the Aragon front. He was killed defending Madrid on 20 November 1936; hundreds of thousands followed his coffin through Barcelona. 'We carry a new world here, in our hearts,' a Canadian journalist quoted him as saying.
reading: Abel Paz, Durruti in the Spanish Revolution (1996)
Hans Magnus Enzensberger, The Short Summer of Anarchy (1972)

entries.title: Federica Montseny (1905–1994)
entries.text: A writer and CNT militant, daughter of anarchist publishers, who in November 1936 became Spain's Minister of Health: the first woman minister in Spanish history, and an anarchist in a government. She pressed for reforms in public health, birth control and the care of the sick and of sex workers, and later regretted, in part, the decision to enter government. She lived in exile in France after the war.
reading: Federica Montseny, Mis primeros cuarenta años (1987)

entries.title: Lucía Sánchez Saornil and Mujeres Libres
entries.text: In 1936 the poet Lucía Sánchez Saornil, with Mercedes Comaposada and Amparo Poch y Gascón, founded Mujeres Libres ('Free Women'), an anarchist women's organization that grew to some twenty thousand members. It ran literacy and job training, child care and a journal, insisting that women's emancipation was not a side issue to be settled after the revolution. Many male comrades disagreed; the CNT never recognized it as an equal branch of the movement.
reading: Martha Ackelsberg, Free Women of Spain (1991)

entries.title: Trust between communes
entries.text: A federation without a centre holds together through relations between its members: shared work, help in bad times, delegates who know each other. Where those relations are weak, communes go their own way, or quarrel over water and land. Anarchists put great weight on this patient building of solidarity.
entries.game: Trust grows from sharing, shared struggle at the front and mediation, and shrinks with hunger, force and neglect. It carries food, militia and ideas between communes, and low trust leads to secession.
reading: Colin Ward, Anarchy in Action (1973)

entries.title: In the shell of the old
entries.text: Anarchists have long held that a free society can't be decreed after a victory; it has to be built in the way people organize now. The Industrial Workers of the World put it in their 1905 preamble: 'forming the structure of the new society within the shell of the old'. The political scientist Carl Boggs later called this 'prefigurative politics' (1977): practising today the relations you want tomorrow, in unions, schools, cooperatives and assemblies. What a movement builds outlasts its victories and defeats: the ateneos and rationalist schools of Spain, the cooperatives and mutual-aid societies, a culture of songs and papers.
entries.game: Legacy paths: each chapter, milestones in mutual aid, the new culture, defence and knowledge. A path reached twice becomes a lasting legacy that shapes every chapter after; in a short game, the legacies are what the movement leaves behind.
reading: Carl Boggs, 'Marxism, Prefigurative Communism, and the Problem of Workers' Control' (1977)
Uri Gordon, Anarchy Alive! (2008)
Colin Ward, Anarchy in Action (1973)

entries.title: Crisis and emergency powers
entries.text: Every revolution meets its emergencies: epidemic, hunger, an offensive, a split within. Each one brings the argument that ordinary freedoms must wait. In Paris in May 1871 the Commune's majority created a Committee of Public Safety; a minority, many of them anarchist-leaning followers of Proudhon, refused it as a return to the methods of the Terror. In Ukraine in the winter of 1919–20, typhus laid low much of Makhno's army. In Catalonia the collectives met shortages with rationing, food committees and supply between villages, while the CNT's leaders entered the government in the name of the war. Anarchists have argued ever since over which emergency measures can be undone, and which become the new order.
entries.game: In campaigns and open starts each chapter ends in a crisis of the age (plague, the hungry years, the great offensive, the counter-revolution within) that builds in three stages. Every policy offered is double-edged: some protect people at a cost in trust or work, others solve the moment and add drift.
reading: Kristin Ross, Communal Luxury (2015)
Alexandre Skirda, Nestor Makhno: Anarchy's Cossack (2004)
Burnett Bolloten, The Spanish Civil War (1991)

entries.title: Factions, and the right to leave
entries.text: A movement without a centre still quarrels. In the CNT the 'treintistas', who signed the Manifesto of the Thirty in 1931 for patient union-building, broke with the insurrectionists of the FAI; some unions left and returned only in 1936. Federalists from Proudhon on held that any member of a federation may leave it, since a union you can't leave is a state. That makes disagreement dangerous but also honest: a faction must be answered, not suppressed.
entries.game: Communes that share a grievance (the centralists, the localists, and others) band into factions. A faction at full strength puts its demand to the congress: concede and pay its price, or refuse and anger its communes, the most aggrieved of which may leave. Delegates can meet a faction and answer it point by point.
reading: Chris Ealham, Anarchism and the City (2010)
Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, The Principle of Federation (1863)

entries.title: Allies of convenience
entries.text: Anarchists have rarely fought alone. Makhno's Insurgent Army allied with the Bolsheviks three times against the Whites; after the last victory, in November 1920, the Red Army turned on it and shot its delegates. In Catalonia the CNT fought beside the Republic and the communist party against Franco while the communists, armed by the Soviet Union, gained ground at its expense; in May 1937 the quarrel broke into street fighting in Barcelona, the May Days. Alliances bring arms and numbers, and a struggle no one side can win outright.
entries.game: The struggle between allies: tension with the movement's allies of convenience rises with the party's growth and a war going badly, and falls with cooperation. At its height it breaks into barricades; kept low for long, the allies recognize the collectives.
reading: Peter Arshinov, History of the Makhnovist Movement (1923)
George Orwell, Homage to Catalonia (1938)

entries.title: Fields, factories and workshops
entries.text: Peter Kropotkin argued in Fields, Factories and Workshops (1899) that regions and people should not be locked into one kind of work: farming and industry, manual and mental labour, could be combined, and a region could feed and clothe itself. In practice federations did specialize. Aragon's collectivized villages sent grain to Barcelona's factories, which sent tools and cloth back, a trade run through union and collective committees. The question is how far to divide work without dividing people.
entries.game: A commune's focus: granary, workshop, fort town, schoolhouse or junction. Each gives more of one thing for a little less of others; the assembly decides, and keeps its choice at least a season.
reading: Peter Kropotkin, Fields, Factories and Workshops (1899)
Sam Dolgoff (ed.), The Anarchist Collectives (1974)

entries.title: Refugees and the rear
entries.text: Wars move people. As Franco's armies advanced, Republican Catalonia took in refugees from across Spain: some 300,000 by the end of 1936, about 700,000 by March 1938, and by most estimates around a million by the end of that year, housed by collectives, unions and families. In Ukraine the Makhnovist army moved with its wagons through villages that fed and hid it. Sheltering refugees is mutual aid at its hardest: more mouths, fewer stores, and newcomers who need time before they can share the work.
entries.game: Population: communes grow when fed and well and shrink in misery; the fighting kills; when a town loses ground or falls, its people flee to the free communes next to it, more to those they trust. Refugees eat at once and join the militia only once they've settled.
reading: Michael Seidman, Republic of Egos (2002)
Helen Graham, The Spanish Republic at War (2002)

entries.title: Festivals and the culture of the movement
entries.text: Anarchism was a way of life as well as a programme: ateneos with libraries and evening classes, theatre groups, excursions, hiking clubs, choirs, newspapers read aloud in workshops. Its songs ('A las barricadas', the Makhnovists' marches) and its festivals mattered. On 16 May 1871 the Paris Commune pulled down the Vendôme Column, Napoleon's monument, as a public festival; that summer of 1936 Barcelona's streets were full of meetings, posters and dances. Joy was part of the argument.
entries.game: Every year the movement marks the anniversary of its rising, and liberation when it comes: celebrate across the federation (influence and food, for enthusiasm, trust and culture), modestly, or not at all. The towns are dressed in flags and lanterns while it lasts.
reading: Kristin Ross, Communal Luxury (2015)
Chris Ealham, Anarchism and the City (2010)

entries.title: Can a stateless society defend itself?
entries.text: The objection: a free society will be overrun by the first disciplined army, so it must build one, and an army needs a command, and a command becomes a state. Engels argued in 'On Authority' (1872) that a revolution is 'the most authoritarian thing there is'. The anarchist answers: militias with elected officers and voluntary discipline (the Durruti Column, Makhno's Insurgent Army, which held off much larger armies for years); guerrilla war and the support of the population; and the warning that an army built in the state's image brings back the state. Honest accounts admit the record is mixed: the Spanish militias were militarized into the Republic's army in 1937, and the Makhnovists were finally crushed by the Red Army.
entries.game: The front is where the game presses hardest: war committees, conscription, emergency powers and commissars all strengthen defence and push drift. Volunteers, defensive campaigns, fortifications and the movement's spirit are the anarchist way, and they are slower.
reading: Friedrich Engels, 'On Authority' (1872)
Abel Paz, Durruti in the Spanish Revolution (1996)
Peter Arshinov, History of the Makhnovist Movement (1923)

entries.title: Coordination at scale
entries.text: The objection: a few villages can run themselves by assembly, but a modern economy of millions can't; it needs prices and markets (as Friedrich Hayek argued about knowledge spread among millions) or a central plan, and both need authority. Engels added that a factory's machinery imposes its own discipline. The anarchist answers: federation, with assemblies sending mandated, recallable delegates to regional and industrial councils; statistics gathered from below; and research on how communities manage shared resources without states or markets, such as Elinor Ostrom's Governing the Commons (1990). Proposals like participatory economics (Michael Albert and Robin Hahnel, 1991) try to show how far it could go. The largest working examples have been regional, and short-lived.
entries.game: Coordination costs rise as the federation grows, and big federal projects add drift. Trust, the federal pool, railways and organizational techniques keep a large federation working without a centre.
reading: Elinor Ostrom, Governing the Commons (1990)
Michael Albert and Robin Hahnel, The Political Economy of Participatory Economics (1991)
Friedrich Hayek, 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945)

entries.title: Free riders, and those who won't join
entries.text: The objection: without enforcement, some will take without giving, and those who won't join will be pressed to. Both happened. Collectives complained of members who shirked; and in Aragon some peasants said they were pushed into collectives by militia columns, a charge historians still argue over; the Republic's army broke up the Council of Aragon in August 1937. The anarchist answers: free association means the right to stay out (in most Aragon collectives, 'individualists' kept as much land as their family could work, though they could hire no labour); social pressure is itself a danger to watch; and accounting in labour-time and open books make shirking visible without police.
entries.game: Free-riding is in the economy: a commune that takes more than it gives is resented, more so where people are individualist, and trust falls. Political education, labour-time accounting and, grimly, police reduce it; collectivization by plan rather than by assent costs trust.
reading: Graham Kelsey, Anarchosyndicalism, Libertarianism and the State (1991)
Michael Seidman, Workers Against Work (1991)

entries.title: Human nature
entries.text: The objection: people are selfish and violent, and only a state holds them in check (Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan, 1651). Kropotkin answered Thomas Huxley's 'The Struggle for Existence' (1888) with Mutual Aid (1902), gathering evidence that cooperation within species is a factor of evolution as strong as competition. Malatesta turned the objection round: precisely because people are not angels, no one should be trusted with power over others. Most anarchists don't claim people are naturally good, only that institutions shape which side of us wins.
entries.game: The game doesn't assume goodness. Communes hoard, free-ride, quarrel and secede; figures grow ambitious. What holds the federation together is built (trust, education, culture) and can be lost.
reading: Peter Kropotkin, Mutual Aid (1902)
Errico Malatesta, Anarchy (1891)
Thomas Hobbes, Leviathan (1651)

entries.title: Anarchists and Marxists
entries.text: Both wanted a classless society; they split over the road. Marx and Engels held that the workers must first take the state (the 'dictatorship of the proletariat'), which would then wither away. Bakunin answered that a workers' state would become the rule of a new minority, 'a red bureaucracy'. The quarrel split the First International; Bakunin was expelled at The Hague in 1872. Lenin's The State and Revolution (1917) promised the withering away; anarchists pointed to what followed, the Cheka, the suppression of the Kronstadt sailors in 1921 and of the Makhnovists. Marxists reply that the anarchists' revolutions were defeated because they refused to organize power.
entries.game: The party is the game's rival: its cells add drift and grow in hard times, its patrons abroad offer arms with commissars attached, and at the end of the drift track a party state takes over.
reading: Mikhail Bakunin, Statism and Anarchy (1873)
V. I. Lenin, The State and Revolution (1917)
Paul Avrich, Kronstadt 1921 (1970)

entries.title: Rights without a state?
entries.text: The liberal objection: without a state, who protects rights, settles disputes and enforces agreements? Robert Nozick argued in Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974) that protective associations would grow into a minimal state anyway. Anarchists answer that states are the great violators of rights, that most disputes are settled without them even now, and that rights can be upheld by free associations and federal arbitration. A note on names: a few libertarians since Murray Rothbard call themselves 'anarcho-capitalists'; most of the anarchist tradition rejects the label, holding that private property in land and workplaces is itself a form of rule.
entries.game: The game models the anarchist answer: communes settle quarrels through mediation and congresses, and the federation holds by trust rather than law. Whether that would be enough is what each game tests.
reading: Robert Nozick, Anarchy, State, and Utopia (1974)
Robert Paul Wolff, In Defense of Anarchism (1970)
Peter Marshall, Demanding the Impossible (1992)

entries.title: Anarchism in East Asia
entries.text: In Japan, Kōtoku Shūsui turned to anarchism after prison and was executed in 1911 in the High Treason Incident; Ōsugi Sakae and the feminist writer Itō Noe were murdered by military police in the chaos after the 1923 Kantō earthquake. Chinese anarchists in Paris and Tokyo from 1907 (Li Shizeng and Wu Zhihui's New Century; He Zhen's feminist Natural Justice) and later Shifu in Guangzhou spread the ideas widely, and anarchism shaped the May Fourth generation; the novelist Ba Jin took the 'Jin' of his pen name from Kropotkin, whom he was translating; the 'Ba' is often traced to Bakunin, though he later said it honoured a classmate. Korean anarchists exiled in Manchuria ran the Shinmin autonomous region in 1929–1931, until the region was overrun.
entries.game: The open world lets you start the movement anywhere: these histories show it was never only European.
reading: Arif Dirlik, Anarchism in the Chinese Revolution (1991)
Sho Konishi, Anarchist Modernity (2013)
Dongyoun Hwang, Anarchism in Korea (2016)

entries.title: Anarchism in Latin America
entries.text: Anarchism came to Latin America with Spanish and Italian workers and took root. Argentina's FORA, founded in 1901, declared for anarchist communism in 1905 and led great strikes; the Tragic Week in Buenos Aires (1919) and the shooting of striking farmhands in Patagonia (1920–22) were its bloodiest defeats. In Mexico Ricardo Flores Magón's Mexican Liberal Party, anarchist in all but name, rose in 1911 and briefly held towns in Baja California under the slogan 'Land and Liberty'. A general strike shut São Paulo in 1917. After Argentina's crash of 2001, workers took over closed factories and ran them themselves, the empresas recuperadas, under the banner of horizontalidad.
entries.game: Open starts in the Americas raise the movement among workers who once flew its flag.
reading: Geoffroy de Laforcade and Kirwin Shaffer (eds.), In Defiance of Boundaries (2015)
Marina Sitrin, Horizontalism (2006)

entries.title: The Zapatistas
entries.text: On 1 January 1994 the Zapatista Army of National Liberation (EZLN) rose in Chiapas, Mexico. Since then indigenous communities have governed autonomous municipalities through assemblies and rotating councils, organized from 2003 into caracoles with 'good government' councils. In 2023, amid rising cartel violence, they dissolved the autonomous municipalities and councils in favour of thousands of local autonomous governments, a further decentralization. Their principle, mandar obedeciendo ('to lead by obeying'), is close to the anarchist imperative mandate, though the Zapatistas draw on Mayan traditions and do not call themselves anarchists. They have kept schools, clinics and cooperatives going for three decades under military pressure.
entries.game: The game's assemblies, recallable delegates and rotation are the same practices; the Zapatistas show them lasting decades, at the scale of a region.
reading: Alex Khasnabish, Zapatismo Beyond Borders (2008)
Subcomandante Marcos, Our Word Is Our Weapon (2001)

entries.title: Democratic confederalism in north-east Syria
entries.text: Since 2012 the Kurdish-led regions of north-east Syria (Rojava) have built a system of communes and councils with male and female co-chairs at every level, inspired by Abdullah Öcalan's 'democratic confederalism', which he drew in prison from Murray Bookchin's libertarian municipalism. Women's defence units fought the Islamic State. Supporters see a stateless democracy built in war; critics point to the dominant role of one party, conscription and the pressures of war. It is not an anarchist project, but anarchists have argued over it more than any other living experiment.
entries.game: A federation of communes at war, with the drift the war brings: the game's central tension, in the present day.
reading: Michael Knapp, Anja Flach and Ercan Ayboga, Revolution in Rojava (2016)
Murray Bookchin, The Next Revolution (2015)

entries.title: Anarchism today
entries.text: Anarchist ideas are now as much a way of organizing as a programme. Food Not Bombs (from 1980) shares food in hundreds of cities; the Common Ground Collective organized relief after Hurricane Katrina (2005) and Occupy Sandy after the 2012 storm; Occupy Wall Street (2011) ran its camps by general assembly and consensus, as did the squares of Spain and Greece. In 2020, mutual-aid networks sprang up in thousands of neighbourhoods during the pandemic. Many who use these methods don't call themselves anarchists; the anthropologist David Graeber argued that this is how anarchism mostly lives, as practice rather than label.
entries.game: Mutual aid, assemblies and trust are the game's working parts; these movements are what they look like now.
reading: David Graeber, Fragments of an Anarchist Anthropology (2004)
Dean Spade, Mutual Aid (2020)
Scott Crow, Black Flags and Windmills (2011)
